title: Male Nervous System Anatomy: Whole-Body & Pelvic Nerves
description: Explore male nervous system anatomy from the brain and spinal cord to major limb plexuses, pudendal nerve paths, prostatic plexuses, and cavernous bundles.
h1: Male Nervous System Anatomy: Whole-Body Tracts and Pelvic Nerves
blurb: Whole-body central and peripheral nerve pathways on the male figure, highlighting limb plexuses alongside prostatic, cavernous, and pudendal pelvic nerves.
lead: While the brain, spinal cord, and limb plexuses follow a shared human plan, pelvic autonomic plexuses and terminal pudendal branches trace sex-specific targets. In this illustrated guide to male nervous system anatomy, we examine 20 documented structures—including brain, spinal cord, cervical plexus, brachial plexus—linking regional topography, tissue architecture, physiological mechanisms, and clinical reasoning.
overview: While the brain, spinal cord, and limb plexuses follow a shared human plan, pelvic autonomic plexuses and terminal pudendal branches trace sex-specific targets. This male figure orients the shared brain, spinal and peripheral nerve plan. The additional study structures focus on nerves to the prostate, penis and perineum. Structurally, the brain (Encephalon) comprises cerebrum, cerebellum and brainstem inside the cranial vault. Physiologically, the brain governs integration, consciousness, motor planning and autonomic control. Structurally, the spinal cord (Medulla spinalis) comprises 31-segment cord from foramen magnum to L1–L2. Physiologically, the spinal cord governs two-way tracts plus segmental reflex circuits. Structurally, the cervical plexus (Plexus cervicalis (C1–C4)) comprises nerve network in the posterior triangle of the neck. Physiologically, the cervical plexus governs neck muscles and skin; phrenic nerve to diaphragm. Structurally, the brachial plexus (Plexus brachialis (C5–T1)) comprises roots-trunks-divisions-cords-branches behind the clavicle. Physiologically, the brachial plexus governs all motor and sensory supply of the upper limb. Structurally, the intercostal nerves (Nn. intercostales (T1–T11)) comprises ventral rami running in subcostal grooves. Physiologically, the intercostal nerves governs chest-wall muscles and segmental skin band. Structurally, the lumbar plexus (Plexus lumbalis (L1–L4)) comprises network within psoas major. Physiologically, the lumbar plexus governs anterior thigh and medial leg supply.

questions.question: Is the male nervous system built differently from the female nervous system?
questions.answer: The main brain, spinal cord and peripheral nerve plan is shared. A male-focused pelvic view highlights branches serving the prostate, penis and scrotum rather than implying separate male brain or spinal pathways. The pudendal nerve is paired somatic S2–S4 nerve passes through the pudendal canal toward the perineum. Physiologically, the pudendal nerve supplies external genital and perineal sensation plus motor branches to sphincters.

questions.question: Which nerves contribute to penile erection?
questions.answer: Autonomic cavernous nerves arising from the prostatic plexus influence penile smooth muscle and blood flow. Somatic sensation from the penis is carried largely through the dorsal nerve of the penis, a pudendal branch. The cavernous nerves of penis is small autonomic branches run from the prostatic plexus toward penile erectile tissue. Physiologically, the cavernous nerves of penis regulate erectile smooth muscle and arterial inflow.

questions.question: What is the pudendal nerve in the male pelvis?
questions.answer: The pudendal nerve derives from sacral segments S2–S4 and supplies much of the perineum. Its branches include the inferior rectal, perineal and dorsal penile nerves; these are distinct from pelvic autonomic nerves. Structurally, the pelvic splanchnic nerves comprises parasympathetic fibers from sacral levels S2–S4 travel to pelvic autonomic plexuses. Physiologically, the pelvic splanchnic nerves governs reach bladder, rectal and reproductive pelvic organ targets.

questions.question: How do pelvic splanchnic nerves differ from hypogastric nerves?
questions.answer: Pelvic splanchnic nerves carry sacral parasympathetic fibers from S2–S4 into pelvic plexuses. Hypogastric nerves convey predominantly sympathetic pathways from higher plexuses; both contribute to pelvic organ innervation. The inferior hypogastric plexus is paired networks on the lateral walls of the rectum combine sympathetic and parasympathetic fibers. Physiologically, the inferior hypogastric plexus governs distribute autonomic pathways to pelvic organs.

questions.question: Can the full-body male nerve picture show individual cavernous nerves?
questions.answer: No. It is an orientation image for major nervous-system routes. Cavernous and prostatic plexus branches are described as unpinned study structures rather than falsely marked on a whole-body plate. Structurally, the prostatic plexus comprises autonomic branches of the inferior hypogastric plexus course along the prostate. Physiologically, the prostatic plexus governs distribute fibers to the prostate and continue toward penile erectile tissue.
